claims.text: Coupled tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by mechanical removal of the protective passive oxide layer.
Mechanical removal of the passive oxide exposes fresh, more reactive metal surfaces.
Exposure of fresh metal by wear accelerates localized corrosion.
The initial high-entropy alloy has a naturally formed passive oxide film in the corrosive environment.
Passive-oxide integrity is the structural mediator of the coupled response.
Wear disrupts and removes the protective oxide film.
The metal beneath the passive film is more susceptible to corrosion than the film-covered surface.
Localized corrosion further degrades wear-exposed areas.
The balance between wear-induced film damage and repassivation controls overall degradation.
Total degradation under tribo-corrosion will exceed the nominal sum of degradation measured in isolated wear and corrosion tests.
The corrosion component will be greater inside wear tracks than in regions not exposed to wear.
Tribo-corrosion will cause more rapid damage than static corrosion with an intact passive film.
The prediction applies when the passive film protects under static conditions but is vulnerable to mechanical removal.
The prediction may fail when the passive film is extremely resistant to wear.
The prediction may fail when repassivation is sufficiently rapid.
Samples with enhanced oxide stability should exhibit reduced degradation or less localization of corrosion in wear tracks relative to baseline samples.
A lack of statistically significant improvement from enhanced oxide stability would falsify the claim that oxide removal is the dominant tribo-corrosion mechanism.
